prompt.en: Two stations confirm a contact near midnight, one in Atlantic Canada and one in British Columbia. Which log habit best prevents later date confusion?

text.en: Record the UTC date as well as the UTC time for the contact.
Use only the local date of the operator who sent the stronger signal report.
Omit the date if both stations remember the band and mode.
Let each station choose its own local date because confirmations never compare dates.

explanation.en: UTC works best when the date and time travel together. Near local midnight, the same contact may fall on different local dates for different operators.

prompt.en: An operator in Halifax uses an azimuthal map centred on Toronto to aim a beam from home. What should they predict?

text.en: The bearings radiate correctly from Toronto, so the map is not centred for Halifax station bearings.
The map automatically converts every bearing to Halifax because azimuthal maps are independent of centre point.
The map is useful only for grid-square codes and cannot show bearings from any centre.
The map can aim the Halifax antenna only after the operator changes the UTC offset.

explanation.en: An azimuthal map shows bearings from its centre. For station bearings from Halifax, the centre needs to be Halifax or the operator needs another bearing source.

prompt.en: A rover is asked for a grid square during a VHF event and replies with the compass heading of their antenna. What is the error?

text.en: A grid square is a location code; antenna heading is a separate bearing.
Antenna heading is correct if it is sent in UTC rather than local time.
A grid square should be replaced by a QSL card because both are proof of bearing.
A grid square is only the name of the map projection and never describes station location.

explanation.en: The requested grid square identifies location in compact form. Bearing is a direction from a station or map centre, not the locator itself.
